screens.title: Introduction to Asynchronous JavaScript and Promises
screens.narratorSegment: In this opening lesson you'll see why asynchronous programming is essential for modern JavaScript and especially for mobile apps built with React Native. JavaScript runs on a single thread, so long operations like network requests would otherwise block the main thread and freeze the interface. We'll explore the evolution from callbacks, with their readability problems, to Promises that model eventual results, and finally to async and await which let you write asynchronous logic in a style that reads like synchronous code. I'll give you concrete examples you can run, show common mistakes that cause subtle bugs, and explain practical patterns for fetching data, updating UI state, and handling errors. By the end of the chapter you will recognize when an operation should be asynchronous, know the three Promise states, be able to chain Promises or refactor them with async/await, and apply try... catch to avoid unhandled rejections. As you work through the examples, ask yourself how each pattern affects readability, error handling, and the user's experience.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introduction
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Introduction to Asynchronous JavaScript and Promises

Understand why JavaScript needs asynchronous patterns for network calls and responsive UIs, then learn Promises and async/await to write maintainable code.

In this lesson
Synchronous vs asynchronous behavior and why blocking is harmful for apps.
Coming up
Callbacks, Promise states and chaining, then async/await with error handling.
Hands-on
A simulated login using async/await to practice loading and error handling.
Why this matters

Mobile apps must remain responsive while performing network I/O. Choosing clear async patterns reduces bugs and improves maintainability.

Concept map
Callbacks → Promises → async/await
Callbacks: simple, but leads to nested code for sequential tasks.
Promises: model a future result with pending, fulfilled, rejected.
async/await: syntactic sugar over Promises for cleaner control flow.
Quick topics
Promise states, chaining with then/catch, refactoring into async/await, handling errors with try...catch.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus on practical skills for everyday React Native development. First, you'll be able to distinguish synchronous from asynchronous programming, so you can predict when code will block the UI and when it will allow the app to continue responding. Second, you'll understand why network requests must be asynchronous and how that improves user experience. Third, you'll be introduced to Promises: you'll learn their three states and how attaching handlers with then and catch creates readable chains. Lastly in this screen you will see how async functions work and why await pauses execution only inside that function, letting you write code that looks sequential while still executing without blocking the main thread. Each objective ties to real tasks like fetching profiles, updating loading state, and handling failures gracefully. Practice these objectives through examples and the hands-on simulated login activity so you can apply them in your own projects.

screens.narratorSegment: These secondary objectives focus on practical application and safe coding habits. You'll implement async/await to make sequences of network requests readable while keeping error handling explicit. You'll also learn to identify common pitfalls such as forgetting to await a Promise, which leaves you operating on a Promise object instead of its resolved value, and failing to catch rejections which can cause unhandled errors. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Skills & Pitfalls
01 — Apply async/await

Refactor Promise chains into async functions to make sequential logic read like synchronous code while keeping non-blocking behavior.

Mnemonic: think of await as a pause inside an async bubble — it doesn't freeze the whole app, only the function execution.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
02 — Avoid forgetting await

Always await promise-returning calls when you need their results. Otherwise you'll operate on a Promise object instead of the value you expect.

Mnemonic: missing await is like leaving a package unopened — the content is still inside the Promise.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
03 — Handle errors explicitly

Use catch or try...catch to handle rejected Promises so the app doesn't surface unhandled rejections to users or crash in production.

Mnemonic: every await should be inside a try or paired with a catch somewhere in the chain.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
04 — Manage loading state

Set loading flags before awaiting network calls and reset them in finally blocks so the UI always reflects the operation's status.

Mnemonic: start loader, await result, stop loader in finally.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

screens.title: Synchronous JavaScript and the blocking problem
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: synchronous JavaScript executes statements one after another on a single thread. That means each operation must finish before the next begins. This model is simple and predictable, but it creates a real problem for long-running tasks like network requests or heavy computations. If the code waits synchronously for a response, the main thread becomes blocked and the user interface stops responding — buttons don't react, animations pause, and the app feels frozen. A concrete example is a mobile app that performs a large fetch operation synchronously; users would see a frozen screen until the network call completes. A common misconception is thinking long tasks automatically run on another thread; in JavaScript they do not by default. The practical takeaway is to avoid synchronous waits for input and output and instead use asynchronous patterns to let the app continue handling input and rendering while the operation completes. For your React Native apps, this keeps the UI smooth even when waiting for remote data. Ask yourself: which parts of your app should never block the main thread?

keyIdea.text: Synchronous execution runs line-by-line on one thread; long operations can freeze the UI unless handled asynchronously.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Synchronous Execution
Definition

Synchronous JavaScript

Code runs sequentially on a single thread. Each step must finish before the next begins, which is predictable but prone to blocking for long operations.

Example scenario: a fetch that waits synchronously would freeze the UI until the response arrives.
Misconception: assuming UI tasks run on a separate thread by default.
Key Takeaway

Avoid synchronous waits for I/O in apps that must remain responsive.

Concrete Example

Imagine a mobile screen that starts a network request and blocks until the response returns. Users can't tap back, animations freeze, and the app feels broken. Using asynchronous calls releases the main thread while the request completes.

Check your understanding
  • Is a network fetch synchronous or asynchronous by default? (Asynchronous.)
  • What happens if a long task blocks the main thread? (UI freezes.)

screens.title: Callbacks and callback hell
screens.narratorSegment: Callbacks are functions passed into other functions to run after an operation completes. They were the earliest pattern for async work in JavaScript and remain useful for simple cases. A concrete example is providing a callback to a network helper so it runs when the response arrives. However, a common pitfall appears when you sequence several dependent asynchronous tasks with callbacks. Fetching a user, then that user's posts, then comments for each post can lead to deeply nested callbacks — a pattern often called callback hell or the pyramid of doom. This nesting makes code harder to read and harder to reason about, and it becomes error-prone when you need to handle failures or cleanup. A common misconception is thinking we can easily flatten callbacks with simple refactoring; in practice, error handling and sequential dependencies force nesting unless a structured abstraction is used. The practical fix is to adopt Promises or async/await which flatten control flow. As you work on exercises, identify nested callbacks and consider how Promise chaining or async/await would convert them into a linear sequence. Callbacks and callback hell means callbacks work, but deep nesting makes maintenance and error handling difficult—prefer promises or async/await for complex sequences.. In practical terms, how nested callbacks spiral and why they are hard to maintain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Callbacks
How callbacks work

A callback is a function passed into another function and executed when an async operation completes. They are simple for single asynchronous tasks but scale poorly when tasks are sequential and dependent.

Nested example (conceptual)
fetchUser(function(user){
  fetchPosts(user.id, function(posts){
    posts.forEach(function(post){
      fetchComments(post.id, function(comments){
        // deeply nested callbacks
      });
    });
  });
});
Problems & remedy
  • Readability suffers as indentation grows.
  • Error handling becomes fragmented across many callbacks.
  • Refactor into Promises or async/await to flatten control flow and centralize error handling.
Pro tip

When you see nested callbacks, pause and refactor into Promises or async/await to simplify reasoning and error paths.

screens.title: Promises: states and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. At any time a Promise is in one of three states. Pending is the initial state while the operation is in progress. Fulfilled means the operation completed successfully and a value is available. Rejected means the operation failed and an error is available. Once a Promise settles to fulfilled or rejected it cannot change state again. This makes Promises predictable for handling results. You attach handlers using then for success and catch for failure. For example, a fetch call returns a Promise that resolves to a response. Chaining then calls lets you pass the result along to the next handler, creating sequential flows without nested callbacks. A common misconception is treating Promises like callbacks — Promises are objects that you attach handlers to, not just functions passed downward. Remember: Promises are fundamental building blocks for composing asynchronous operations safely and readably. Promises: states and behavior means pending → fulfilled or rejected; once settled a promise's state is final and handlers can be attached with then and catch.. In practical terms, an object that represents a future result: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Promises
What is a Promise?

A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. It exposes a predictable lifecycle and lets you attach success and error handlers.

Pending
Operation in progress; no result yet.
Fulfilled
Operation completed successfully; value available.
Rejected
Operation failed; error available.
Attach handlers
fetch('url')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error(error));
Chain then calls to sequence steps. Use catch to centralize error handling. Remember a settled Promise is immutable in state.

screens.title: Promise chaining for sequential operations
screens.narratorSegment: Promise chaining is a technique that sequences asynchronous steps by returning values or Promises from then handlers. The core claim is simple: each then receives the previous result and may return a new value or Promise that becomes the input for the next then. For example, fetch returns a Promise that resolves to a response object; calling response. json() returns another Promise that resolves to parsed data. By chaining these with then, you produce a readable, linear flow for dependent async tasks without nested callbacks. A concrete example from the chapter shows fetch('url'). then(response => response. json()). then(data => console. log(data)). catch(error => console. error(error));. A common misconception is that then always runs synchronously; then handlers run asynchronously after the Promise settles. When chaining many steps, always include catch at the end or attach local catches to handle specific failures. The takeaway is that Promise chaining flattens dependent operations and centralizes error handling, improving readability over nested callbacks. Promise chaining for sequential operations means return values or promises from then to sequence operations; attach catch to handle errors across the chain.. In practical terms, how results flow from one .then() to the next. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Promise Chaining
Pattern

Sequential async operations with then

fetch('url')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error(error));
Each then returns a value or Promise passed to the next then. Place catch at the end to catch any rejection from the chain.
Notes
  • then handlers are asynchronous and run after the Promise settles.
  • Return Promises from then to continue asynchronous sequences.
  • Use catch to centralize error handling; attach specific catches when needed.
Check

If response.json() returns a Promise, what must you do before using the parsed data? Await the Promise or return it in a then so the next handler receives the data.

screens.title: async and await
screens.narratorSegment: async and await provide a more readable way to work with Promises. Declaring a function with the async keyword makes it implicitly return a Promise. Inside that function, await pauses execution until the awaited Promise settles, and then resumes with its resolved value. This pause affects only the async function, not the global execution thread, so the application remains responsive. A concrete example from the chapter shows an async function that awaits a Promise-based delay and logs a success message. Error handling integrates naturally: if an awaited Promise rejects, await throws an exception which you can catch with try... catch just like synchronous code. A common misconception is thinking await blocks the entire app; it only suspends the async function's execution. The clear takeaway is that async/await keeps sequential logic intuitive while preserving non-blocking behavior, making network request code in React Native easier to write and maintain. async and await means async functions return promises; await pauses inside those functions to yield resolved values while keeping the app non-blocking.. In practical terms, syntactic sugar over promises for clearer asynchronous code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › async / await
Syntax
async function fetchDataAsync() {
  try {
    const message = await new Promise((resolve) => {
      setTimeout(() => resolve("Data fetched successfully with async/await!"), 2000);
    });
    console.log(message);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}

fetchDataAsync();
Why use it?
  • Reads like synchronous code, making logic easier to follow.
  • Error handling uses familiar try...catch blocks.
  • Preserves non-blocking behavior because only the async function pauses.
Key Takeaway

Use async/await for sequential async code and wrap awaits in try...catch to handle errors robustly.

screens.title: Converting Promise chains into async/await
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring a Promise chain into async/await preserves the same behavior while simplifying the control flow. The claim is that replacing multiple then handlers with sequential await calls makes the code easier to read and debug. Consider a Promise chain that fetches a resource, parses JSON, and then processes data. With async/await you write the same sequence with clearer variable names, straightforward error handling in try... catch, and no nested callbacks. A concrete corrected example from the chapter highlights a common mistake: forgetting to await a fetch call. The corrected async version awaits the fetch, then awaits response. json(), and wraps both awaits in a try... catch to handle network or parsing errors. A common misconception is that async/await always needs fewer lines; it often uses similar lines but improves clarity, especially when multiple sequential steps depend on each other. The takeaway: when you find long chains of then, consider an async function with await and try... catch for cleaner logic and centralized error handling. Converting Promise chains into async/await means replace sequential .then() operations with await inside an async function and use try...catch to handle errors centrally.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Refactor: .then → async/await
Before (Promise chain)
fetch('https://api.example.com/data')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => handleData(data))
  .catch(error => console.error(error));
After (async/await)
async function loadAndHandle() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data');
    const data = await response.json();
    handleData(data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}
This refactor keeps the same behavior but centralizes error handling and makes the sequence easier to follow and debug.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the most common mistakes you will encounter. First, forgetting to await a Promise-returning function is a frequent slip. The chapter shows an incorrect example where a fetch call is not awaited and the code then calls response. json() on a Promise object — that fails. The fix is to await the fetch to obtain the Response object, then await response. json(). Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Simulated Login
Starter Code
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, Text, Button, ActivityIndicator, StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

const LoginScreen = () => {
  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);

  const simulateLogin = async () => {
    setIsLoading(true);
    setMessage('Logging in...');

    try {
      const response = await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        setTimeout(() => {
          const success = Math.random() > 0.5; // 50% chance of success
          if (success) {
            resolve('Login successful!');
          } else {
            reject('Invalid credentials.');
          }
        }, 3000); // Simulate 3-second network request
      });
      setMessage(response); // Update message with success
    } catch (error) {
      setMessage(`Login Failed: ${error}`); // Update message with error
    } finally {
      setIsLoading(false); // Stop loading regardless of outcome
    }
  };

  return (
    
      Simulated Login
    
  );
};

export default LoginScreen;
Walkthrough
  1. Set isLoading true and show a progress message before the await.
  2. Await a Promise that simulates network latency.
  3. On success, display the resolved message; on failure, display the error inside catch.
  4. Always stop the loader in finally so the UI is consistent.

Modify simulateLogin to accept username and password, and only resolve if username is 'admin' and password is 'password123'.

fullNarratorScript:
In this opening lesson you'll see why asynchronous programming is essential for modern JavaScript and especially for mobile apps built with React Native. JavaScript runs on a single thread, so long operations like network requests would otherwise block the main thread and freeze the interface. We'll explore the evolution from callbacks, with their readability problems, to Promises that model eventual results, and finally to async and await which let you write asynchronous logic in a style that reads like synchronous code. I'll give you concrete examples you can run, show common mistakes that cause subtle bugs, and explain practical patterns for fetching data, updating UI state, and handling errors. By the end of the chapter you will recognize when an operation should be asynchronous, know the three Promise states, be able to chain Promises or refactor them with async/await, and apply try... catch to avoid unhandled rejections. As you work through the examples, ask yourself how each pattern affects readability, error handling, and the user's experience.

These learning objectives focus on practical skills for everyday React Native development. First, you'll be able to distinguish synchronous from asynchronous programming, so you can predict when code will block the UI and when it will allow the app to continue responding. Second, you'll understand why network requests must be asynchronous and how that improves user experience. Third, you'll be introduced to Promises: you'll learn their three states and how attaching handlers with then and catch creates readable chains. Lastly in this screen you will see how async functions work and why await pauses execution only inside that function, letting you write code that looks sequential while still executing without blocking the main thread. Each objective ties to real tasks like fetching profiles, updating loading state, and handling failures gracefully. Practice these objectives through examples and the hands-on simulated login activity so you can apply them in your own projects.

These secondary objectives focus on practical application and safe coding habits. You'll implement async/await to make sequences of network requests readable while keeping error handling explicit. You'll also learn to identify common pitfalls such as forgetting to await a Promise, which leaves you operating on a Promise object instead of its resolved value, and failing to catch rejections which can cause unhandled errors. We'll practice wrapping awaits in try... catch and using finally to manage loading state. Finally, you'll learn to refactor Promise chains into async functions to improve maintainability. Each objective connects to a simple exercise: simulate a delayed login call, update UI loading state, and handle a success or failure outcome so you can see both the pattern and the common mistakes in a safe environment. Skills and pitfalls to watch means write and test small async examples and deliberately trigger errors to learn how try...catch and .catch() behave.. In practical terms, apply patterns and avoid common asynchronous mistakes. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start with a clear definition: synchronous JavaScript executes statements one after another on a single thread. That means each operation must finish before the next begins. This model is simple and predictable, but it creates a real problem for long-running tasks like network requests or heavy computations. If the code waits synchronously for a response, the main thread becomes blocked and the user interface stops responding — buttons don't react, animations pause, and the app feels frozen. A concrete example is a mobile app that performs a large fetch operation synchronously; users would see a frozen screen until the network call completes. A common misconception is thinking long tasks automatically run on another thread; in JavaScript they do not by default. The practical takeaway is to avoid synchronous waits for input and output and instead use asynchronous patterns to let the app continue handling input and rendering while the operation completes. For your React Native apps, this keeps the UI smooth even when waiting for remote data. Ask yourself: which parts of your app should never block the main thread?

Callbacks are functions passed into other functions to run after an operation completes. They were the earliest pattern for async work in JavaScript and remain useful for simple cases. A concrete example is providing a callback to a network helper so it runs when the response arrives. However, a common pitfall appears when you sequence several dependent asynchronous tasks with callbacks. Fetching a user, then that user's posts, then comments for each post can lead to deeply nested callbacks — a pattern often called callback hell or the pyramid of doom. This nesting makes code harder to read and harder to reason about, and it becomes error-prone when you need to handle failures or cleanup. A common misconception is thinking we can easily flatten callbacks with simple refactoring; in practice, error handling and sequential dependencies force nesting unless a structured abstraction is used. The practical fix is to adopt Promises or async/await which flatten control flow. As you work on exercises, identify nested callbacks and consider how Promise chaining or async/await would convert them into a linear sequence. Callbacks and callback hell means callbacks work, but deep nesting makes maintenance and error handling difficult—prefer promises or async/await for complex sequences.. In practical terms, how nested callbacks spiral and why they are hard to maintain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. At any time a Promise is in one of three states. Pending is the initial state while the operation is in progress. Fulfilled means the operation completed successfully and a value is available. Rejected means the operation failed and an error is available. Once a Promise settles to fulfilled or rejected it cannot change state again. This makes Promises predictable for handling results. You attach handlers using then for success and catch for failure. For example, a fetch call returns a Promise that resolves to a response. Chaining then calls lets you pass the result along to the next handler, creating sequential flows without nested callbacks. A common misconception is treating Promises like callbacks — Promises are objects that you attach handlers to, not just functions passed downward. Remember: Promises are fundamental building blocks for composing asynchronous operations safely and readably. Promises: states and behavior means pending → fulfilled or rejected; once settled a promise's state is final and handlers can be attached with then and catch.. In practical terms, an object that represents a future result: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Promise chaining is a technique that sequences asynchronous steps by returning values or Promises from then handlers. The core claim is simple: each then receives the previous result and may return a new value or Promise that becomes the input for the next then. For example, fetch returns a Promise that resolves to a response object; calling response. json() returns another Promise that resolves to parsed data. By chaining these with then, you produce a readable, linear flow for dependent async tasks without nested callbacks. A concrete example from the chapter shows fetch('url'). then(response => response. json()). then(data => console. log(data)). catch(error => console. error(error));. A common misconception is that then always runs synchronously; then handlers run asynchronously after the Promise settles. When chaining many steps, always include catch at the end or attach local catches to handle specific failures. The takeaway is that Promise chaining flattens dependent operations and centralizes error handling, improving readability over nested callbacks. Promise chaining for sequential operations means return values or promises from then to sequence operations; attach catch to handle errors across the chain.. In practical terms, how results flow from one .then() to the next. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

async and await provide a more readable way to work with Promises. Declaring a function with the async keyword makes it implicitly return a Promise. Inside that function, await pauses execution until the awaited Promise settles, and then resumes with its resolved value. This pause affects only the async function, not the global execution thread, so the application remains responsive. A concrete example from the chapter shows an async function that awaits a Promise-based delay and logs a success message. Error handling integrates naturally: if an awaited Promise rejects, await throws an exception which you can catch with try... catch just like synchronous code. A common misconception is thinking await blocks the entire app; it only suspends the async function's execution. The clear takeaway is that async/await keeps sequential logic intuitive while preserving non-blocking behavior, making network request code in React Native easier to write and maintain. async and await means async functions return promises; await pauses inside those functions to yield resolved values while keeping the app non-blocking.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The claim is that replacing multiple then handlers with sequential await calls makes the code easier to read and debug. Consider a Promise chain that fetches a resource, parses JSON, and then processes data. With async/await you write the same sequence with clearer variable names, straightforward error handling in try... catch, and no nested callbacks. To close the chapter, remember three compact ideas. First, synchronous code runs line-by-line and can block the UI; avoid synchronous waits for network or heavy tasks. Second, Promises represent future results with three states — pending, fulfilled, rejected — and let you attach then and catch handlers to manage flows. Third, async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises that makes asynchronous sequences look like synchronous code and integrates with try... catch for clear error handling. Keep these concepts in mind as you implement network requests with loading state and robust error management.
